title: Modified Low-Temperature Scanning Tunneling Microscope for Ultrafast Pump-Probe Spectroscopy
authors: Vibhuti N. Rai, Junyoung Sim, Nils Bogdanoff, Sergey Trishin, Florian Faaber, Paul Wiechers, Caroline Firschke, Tobias Kampfrath, Christian Lotze, Katharina J. Franke
abstract: Combining scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) with terahertz pulses (THz-STM) enables ultrafast dynamics of phonons, spins, and charge carriers to be probed with atomic-scale spatial and sub-picosecond temporal resolution. However, coupling THz radiation into a low-temperature STM junction presents some technical challenges as it requires optical access for laser illumination while maintaining junction stability. Instead of designing a completely new STM head with customized optical access and optics within the ultra-high vacuum chamber, we modified a Besocke "Beetle" style STM with minimal changes of the cryogenic radiation shields. Despite the given geometrical conditions, we achieved efficient coupling of THz and optical pulses to the STM junction while maintaining temperatures below 6 K. We designed the optical setup on a separate laser table, starting with femtosecond laser pulses that are used to generate THz pulses in a LiNbO$_3$ crystal. We show the obtained THz pulse shapes and determine the effective time resolution using cross-correlation measurements. We further demonstrate the stable performance of the modified STM by measuring THz-induced tunneling currents from monolayer molybdenum disulfide (MoS$_2$) grown on Au(111). The resulting current maps resolve atomic-scale contrast revealing a point defect. The measurements confirm efficient THz coupling and stable low-temperature STM operation with atomic resolution.
summary: The authors modified a low-temperature STM to enable Terahertz (THz) pump-probe spectroscopy, allowing the study of ultrafast dynamics at atomic resolution. By efficiently coupling THz pulses into the junction, they demonstrated stable operation and successfully mapped atomic-scale features in MoS2 using THz-induced tunneling currents.
main_problem: The goal is to probe ultrafast dynamics (phonons, spins, charge carriers) at the atomic scale using Scanning Tunneling Microscopy (STM) combined with Terahertz (THz) pulses.
main_result: The modified STM successfully coupled THz and optical pulses while maintaining cryogenic stability, and measurements on MoS2 resolved atomic-scale contrast revealing a point defect.
method: The setup involves generating THz pulses from femtosecond laser pulses in a LiNbO3 crystal and coupling these pulses into the STM junction via minimal modifications to a low-temperature STM head.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a modified low-temperature Besocke "Beetle" style STM operating below 6 K. The system probes the time-varying current induced by the THz field ($	ext{I}(t) = 	ext{I}_b + 	ext{i}_{	ext{THz}}(t)$) in materials like monolayer MoS2.
key_observables: THz-induced tunneling currents, atomic-scale current maps, and the effective time resolution of the THz pulse.
important_parameters: Temperatures below 6 K; sub-picosecond temporal resolution; atomic spatial resolution; THz frequency range ($\sim 0.6$ THz).
main_assumptions: The modifications to the STM are designed to be minimally invasive, preserving the original noise performance and low-temperature baseline.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup of the THz-STM, the optical path for THz generation and characterization (using EOS), and temperature stability measurements confirming the system's operational integrity.
paper_structure: The paper details the engineering modifications required for optical access, describes the THz pulse generation and characterization, and concludes with experimental measurements demonstrating stable, high-resolution THz-induced tunneling spectroscopy on 2D materials.
why_interesting: This work provides an experimental platform to study non-equilibrium, ultrafast dynamics in solid-state systems, which is highly relevant for understanding energy relaxation pathways and quantum coherence in condensed matter.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of the THz-STM. Cross-sectional overview illustrating the path of the THz/optical pulses from outside of the UHV chamber into the STM junction. A collimated THz/optical beam enters the UHV chamber (from right to left) through the quartz window (M1). Thereafter, it passes through the liquid-nitrogen (LN2) and liquid-helium (LHe) radiation shields, respectively. A movable shutter is integrated into the LN2 shield to enable or block the THz/optical beam. Inset (top left): sketch of the shutter mounted on the LN2 shield. Image is not to scale.
